title: Recovering the Quadrivium
author: Daniel Murphy
summary: Daniel Murphy, a math teacher at a Houston liberal arts school, observes that classical schools teach literature, history, and language very differently from district schools while keeping a nearly identical mathematics sequence, and argues that this reveals an inherited, utilitarian understanding of what mathematics is for. He recovers the older answer from Plato's Republic, Nicomachus, and Boethius: the quadrivial arts of arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy study multitude and magnitude and turn the mind from changing appearances toward unchanging truth as preparation for philosophy. He then traces how the Committee of Ten, the Committee of Fifteen, the 1923 MAA report, and the Carnegie Unit fixed practical use and mental discipline as the aims of American school mathematics. Turning to Dorothy Sayers's influential 'Lost Tools of Learning,' he argues that by treating mathematics as a sub-department of logic and never saying what the quadrivium is for, Sayers left classical schools nothing to build on, so they defaulted to the conventional sequence. He closes by noting that the ACCS's 'fourth generation' now names the quadrivium, but insists that recovery requires stating and teaching toward mathematics' philosophical purpose, not just integrating existing courses.
points: Classical schools such as Logos School run the same Arithmetic-to-Calculus sequence as conventional schools, signaling that their math program was inherited rather than designed from classical principles.

For Plato, Nicomachus, and Boethius, the quadrivium's aim is turning the mind toward unchanging truth, so math teaching should convey wonder and understanding rather than mainly drill and application.
Murphy traces modern aims to the Committees of Ten and Fifteen and the 1923 MAA report, which reduced even 'cultural' aims of mathematics to practical ones.
Sayers's description of mathematics as a 'sub-department of Logic' and her silence on the quadrivium's purpose left classical educators without guidance for math curriculum.
Integration of subjects is not enough; schools must be able to say that knowing multitude and magnitude prepares students for philosophy, or reform will only rearrange existing courses.
quotes: The language, literature, and history sequences look nothing like the local district’s, but the mathematics program is nearly indistinguishable from it. It seems that we have inherited a mathematics program designed for practical use and mental discipline.

But most classical schools today look to Dorothy Sayers’ 1947 lecture, The Lost Tools of Learning, for inspiration. Sayers proposed a curriculum based around the trivium, but she all but ignored the quadrivium. To recover the quadrivium we have to ask why we teach mathematics in the first place, and that means looking past Sayers to Plato and his successors, who answered it.
Mathematics education should not aim chiefly at practical usage or training the mind, but at turning students from the changing material world toward what is unchanging and true.

One of my geometry students told me that his favorite moment in the class came after completing a proof from Euclid’s Elements at the board and writing “QED.” When a student reaches that point and sees that the proof is valid and the conclusion could not be otherwise, he has encountered unchanging mathematical truth. He has been turned away from false images toward the things that do not change.

Children form an idea of what mathematics is long before anyone explains it to them. If their early experience is mostly drill and application, they will conclude that utility is the primary purpose. If they experience wonder and understanding, their minds will be purified to see the truth and will be better able to understand the true purpose of mathematics.

The aim of their educational philosophy is practical: preparation for college or preparation for the duties of life. In arithmetic, they recommend “omitting entirely those subjects which perplex and exhaust the pupil without affording any really valuable mental discipline.” Mental discipline was the criterion for content.

Every American body that stated the aims of mathematics named practical use or training of the mind. None of them said that knowing the object of mathematics, multitude and magnitude, is a preparation for philosophy. Until schools and teachers, my own school and myself included, can say this and teach mathematics accordingly, recovering the quadrivium will amount to rearranging the courses we already have.
